sections.html:
The county seat of Stark County, in the southwest corner of North Dakota, is Dickinson, known as the Queen City. It stands at 2,460 feet across about 13.3 square miles, where Interstate 94 crosses ND 22. Getting around without a car is possible: United flies to Denver from the regional airport, Jefferson Lines runs intercity buses, and the dial-a-ride service costs $4.

A parcel may lie within city limits or beyond them in Stark County, and each side has its own permit and code office. Settle that question for your address first.

sections.h2: The oil boom and local housing
sections.html:
Between 2010 and the 2020 census the city's population rose from 17,787 to 25,679, about 44 percent. Streets, water and sewer systems struggled to keep up. A wastewater treatment expansion first budgeted at $12 million ended up at $48 million once population estimates were revised, and impact fees charged on new housing helped cover roads and other infrastructure.

A house bought or built in that stretch can have a messier ownership history than an older one. Owners from those years sometimes land in situations like these:

  • More owed on the loan than planned after repairs or a relocation
  • A vacant house after a job ended
  • Rental tenants who left maintenance undone
  • Heirs scattered across several states

For a price check, use a local appraisal or county records rather than a general claim about the market.

Storms have shaped this city's housing stock. In 1924 a tornado killed nine people, and in 2009 an EF3 tornado damaged over 450 homes and businesses, roughly 100 beyond repair, without injuries. A house that took storm damage needs its insurance paperwork and repair records on file, since buyers and title companies request them.

Winters are cold and the air is dry. The climate is humid continental but milder than Bismarck's, and drought is a genuine risk with only 15.63 inches of precipitation a year at the airport (1991 to 2020). January runs near 16 degrees Fahrenheit and July near 69, with a record low of minus 47 and a record high of 114. Freezing weather usually lasts from September 22 to May 16, nearly eight months, so look hard at the furnace, insulation and pipes before listing. The Southwest Water Authority supplies city water from Lake Sakakawea.

The City of Dickinson adopted the North Dakota State Building Code in 2003, which relies on the International Building, Mechanical, Residential and Property Maintenance Codes. The Building Official supervises inspections and municipal code enforcement.

Work done without a permit, such as a finished basement, a new deck or changed wiring, can be spotted by a buyer's inspector. The inspection hotline is 701-456-7035 (option 1 for building, option 2 for engineering), and the Building Official answers at 701-456-7803. Call before you guess about fees or rental rules.

Rentals and inherited homes raise code questions most often, since the seller may not have been inside for years. Unfinished work does not always stop a cash purchase. Still, share what you know about the house with the buyer.

North Dakota's statewide schedule applies here, with four dates to remember, listed below.

DateWhat happens
December 26Statements mailed
February 15Last day for the 5 percent discount
March 1First installment due
October 15Second installment due

The Primary Residence Credit is worth up to $1,600, applied to the next year's tax, and it requires an application each spring. Homestead credit applications go to the local assessor. For forms and filing dates, call the Stark County Auditor's office, the County Tax Director or the Dickinson City Assessor.

Stark County publishes its levy figures each year. They show dollars raised by each district, not mill rates, so your own bill depends on your parcel's taxable value.

A lender here has to go to court to foreclose. It typically sends a notice 30 to 90 days before suing, and that notice gives you 30 days to bring the loan current. If a foreclosure sale does happen, N.D.C.C. 32-19-18 generally gives a borrower 60 days to redeem, with exceptions for abandoned or agricultural property.

Lenders cannot get a deficiency judgment after foreclosing on residential property of four units or fewer when the owner lives in one unit and the land is up to 40 contiguous acres. A sale before the foreclosure date lets you settle the loan on your own terms. An attorney or a HUD-approved counselor can help you weigh that choice.

sections.h2: Is a cash sale a good fit?
sections.html:
Cash works best for a house that needs repairs, came through an estate, is a rental, or must sell by a certain date. The buyer takes it as it stands, and no lender appraisal gets in the way. For a tidy house with plenty of time, the open market may bring more.

  • Compare what each route costs: commission, repairs and carrying costs.
  • Put your mortgage payoff and any special assessment balance in writing.
  • Decide who pays this year's property tax at closing.

Sellers of homes with up to four units must disclose material facts in writing under Century Code 47-10-02.1, though fiduciaries administering an estate or trust are exempt. We will be upfront about what we can say on price until we have walked through the house.

sections.h2: Selling a rental or inherited house
sections.html:
Many Dickinson houses that come up for sale are rentals or inherited properties. A rental sold with tenants in place should come with the leases and any repair records. A rental that sat empty after the tenants left may need a walk-through first, so you know what condition you are describing. For an inherited house, collect the estate paperwork, the latest property tax statement and any mortgage statement, so that everyone with a say agrees on the payoff before a closing date is set.

If heirs live in different states, one person usually needs authority to sign, and the title company will ask who that is. Settling that early prevents delays, whether you list the house or take a cash offer.

A few records speed up any sale, listed or cash. Put these in one folder:

  • Your mortgage payoff in writing, with the date it runs through
  • Any special assessment balance for the parcel
  • The latest property tax statement, and proof of which installments are paid
  • Insurance and repair records if a storm ever damaged the house
  • Permits for finished basements, decks or wiring work

With these in hand, a buyer or title company can tell you quickly what you will net. Missing permits do not always block a sale, but a buyer's inspector may raise them, so tell the buyer what you know instead of waiting for it to surface.

faqs.q: When are Stark County property taxes due?
faqs.a: Statements are mailed December 26. Paying in full by February 15 earns a 5 percent discount. Otherwise the first installment is due March 1 and the second October 15.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Dickinson house that was damaged in a storm?
faqs.a: Yes. A 2009 EF3 tornado damaged more than 450 homes and businesses here, so buyers know the pattern. Keep your insurance claim records and photographs.

faqs.q: How long do I have to redeem a home after foreclosure?
faqs.a: North Dakota generally allows 60 days after the sale, except for abandoned or agricultural property. Confirm the dates for your case with an attorney.

faqs.q: Do I need a seller disclosure in Dickinson?
faqs.a: For most sales of homes with up to four units, yes: on a written form when an agent is involved, or in writing otherwise. Estate fiduciaries and some family transfers are exempt.

faqs.q: Who do I call about permits for work I did?
faqs.a: Call the inspection hotline at 701-456-7035, or the Building Official at 701-456-7803.
